title: A very present help (Psalm 46)
hook: though the mountains shake into the sea, God is our refuge
tomorrow: create in me a clean heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hart at the water brooks and a singer talking to his own soul. Your line was why so cast down, my soul? Did you ask it gently, and wait for an answer? Day four hundred twenty-three.

Most phones have a place for an emergency contact. One name, one number, for the moment something goes badly wrong and someone else has to make the call. People don't usually pick the most impressive person they know. They pick the one who picks up. The one who has shown up before, at two in the morning, at the side of the road, on moving day. Psalm forty-six is a song about that kind of help. Months ago on this path we met one of its lines, be still. Today, the rest of the song: the earthquake that comes before the stillness, and a river that, on any map of Jerusalem, shouldn't be there.
screen: `AN EMERGENCY CONTACT.` → `THE ONE WHO PICKS UP.` → `A RIVER THAT SHOULDN'T BE THERE.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." In the King James English, very present means near at hand, right there. The Hebrew says it a little differently: a help in troubles, found very much. Found again and again. Help with a track record. Then the song gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." Waters roar, mountains shake, nations rage. Nothing in this psalm pretends trouble isn't real. And right in the middle of the noise, verse four: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Here's the surprise. Jerusalem had no river. It had a spring, the Gihon, and water carried through tunnels, but no river running through its streets. So the psalm sings one anyway. Outside, the sea roars and swallows mountains. Inside, a quiet river makes a city glad. Some readers hear it as a picture of God's presence in the middle of his people. Then verse five: God will help her, "and that right early." In the Hebrew, that's at the turning of the morning. The help arrives as the night ends. Twice the psalm repeats its chorus: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge." And each time, one more word: Selah. Nobody knows for sure what it means. One common guess is a pause in the music. If so, the pause falls right after the line about who's with us.
screen: `HELP FOUND, AGAIN AND AGAIN` · `MOUNTAINS CARRIED INTO THE SEA` · `A RIVER IN A CITY WITHOUT ONE` · `HELP AT THE TURNING OF MORNING` · then, large: `THE LORD OF HOSTS IS WITH US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe through one anxious moment. Sit, and bring to mind one thing that has been making your chest tight. Let it be there, like the roaring water in the psalm. Don't fight it and don't solve it. Then look for the river. Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out longer than it came in. Again. Feel where your body is held up: the chair, the floor. If you pray, you can say the first verse once, slowly: God is our refuge and strength. If you don't, just keep breathing, long and slow, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Selah. The mysterious word that follows this psalm's refrain twice, maybe marking a pause in the music right after who is with us.
Your line: found very much. Today, when anxiety rises, take three slow breaths before anything else, and then notice who or what is actually near you. Day four hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 423 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CREATE IN ME A CLEAN HEART.`

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of disaster, war or fear, and it lies behind Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God."

fork.setup: the earth shakes, the waters roar, the nations rage. you're writing the psalm. what do you sing about next?
options: how high the waves are getting.
a quiet river that makes the city glad.
a plan to run for the hills.
fork.reveal: verse 4: "there is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Jerusalem had no river. the psalm sings one into the middle of the storm.

original.note: Hebrew: help. the psalm calls God a help in troubles, "found very much": help with a track record.

trapdoor: what you thought: a soft promise that nothing bad will happen.
what it means: a song sung while the ground shakes. trouble is real, and help is near.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew says a help in troubles "found very much", and verse 5's "right early" is literally at the turning of the morning.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook drops the hospital image (also days 416, 418) and the superlative "its most famous verse"; cut the uncited "In 1611"; "many readers" and "many think" softened; garbled "Which may be the best place to put it" rewritten; howItsDone "often" and "many churches" removed.
Day 145 already taught Psalm 46:10 (be still) and Luther's hymn; this day deliberately takes verses 1–7 instead and mentions Luther only in howItsDone.
'Found very much' (nimtsa me'od) as a literal rendering of 46:1b; confirm.
Claim that Jerusalem had no river, only the Gihon spring and its tunnels (Hezekiah's tunnel, 2 Chronicles 32:30). Confirm wording.
'Right early' = Hebrew lifnot boqer, 'at the turning of morning'. Confirm.
Selah: meaning uncertain; 'many think it marked a pause' is the common view. Confirm.
